title: ServiceAccounts, Authentication, Authorization and Admission Control

header.html: Understand authentication, authorization and admission control; Understand ServiceAccounts

toc.title: Every API request passes three gates

html:
1Every API request passes three gates

When kubectl or a Pod calls the API server, the request is checked in order:

Gate Question Typical answer If it fails
1. Authentication who are you? a client certificate, a bearer token (a ServiceAccount token), an OIDC token 401 Unauthorized
2. Authorization may you do this to this object? RBAC rules (a Role or ClusterRole bound to you) 403 Forbidden
3. Admission control is this object acceptable (and may it be changed)? mutating and validating admission: defaults, quotas, Pod Security an error naming the policy

Authentication and authorization decide about the caller; admission decides about the object. Admission runs only for create, update and delete, and a request that fails authorization never reaches it.

2Authentication: users and ServiceAccounts

Kubernetes has no user objects. A person is whoever the cluster's authenticator recognizes (a certificate with CN=jane, an OIDC identity). Pods authenticate with a ServiceAccount, an object in a namespace. Its identity is system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.

kubectl auth whoami shows who the cluster thinks you are.

3ServiceAccounts in Pods

Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount, and a Pod without serviceAccountName uses it. A Pod's containers get a short-lived token through a projected volume at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ (files token, ca.crt, namespace). Code in the Pod uses it to call the API server at https://kubernetes.default.svc.

k create serviceaccount app-sa -n auth
k run client --image=busybox:1.36 -n auth --dry-run=client -o yaml -- sleep 3600 > pod.yaml
# in pod.yaml, under spec:   serviceAccountName: app-sa

spec:
  serviceAccountName: app-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false     # do not mount the token at all
Setting Effect
spec.serviceAccountName the identity of the Pod (cannot change on a running Pod)
spec.automountServiceAccountToken: false the Pod gets no token; set it on Pods that never call the API
serviceAccount.automountServiceAccountToken: false the same default for every Pod using that ServiceAccount (a Pod can override)
imagePullSecrets on a ServiceAccount every Pod using it can pull from that registry

Tokens on demand. k create token app-sa -n auth --duration=2h prints a token that expires (default one hour). Use it with --token or in an Authorization: Bearer ... header. These tokens are signed JWTs: the middle part decodes to the sub, iat and exp claims.

4Authorization with RBAC

RBAC answers "who may do what". It has four objects:

Object Scope Purpose
Role one namespace a list of rules: verbs on resources
ClusterRole whole cluster the same, plus non-namespaced resources (nodes) and cluster-wide use
RoleBinding one namespace gives a Role or a ClusterRole to subjects in that namespace
ClusterRoleBinding whole cluster gives a ClusterRole to subjects in every namespace 
k create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n auth
k create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=auth:app-sa -n auth
k create clusterrole deploy-viewer --verb=get,list --resource=deployments
k create rolebinding view-deploys --clusterrole=deploy-viewer --serviceaccount=auth:app-sa -n auth

A RoleBinding that points at a ClusterRole is the neat way to reuse a rule set in one namespace: the permissions apply only in the binding's namespace. Verbs: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection. A subject is a User, a Group or a ServiceAccount (--serviceaccount=<namespace>:<name>, --user=jane, --group=devs).

Check access with can-i:

k auth can-i list pods -n auth --as=system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa     # yes or no
k auth can-i delete pods -n auth --as=system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa
k auth can-i --list -n auth --as=system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa        # everything it may do

RBAC is additive: there are no deny rules. If you cannot reach something, add a rule; to remove access, delete the binding. The roleRef of a binding cannot be edited: delete and recreate it.

A 403 inside a Pod

A Pod that calls the API and gets 403 Forbidden runs under a ServiceAccount without the right rule. The error text names the user and the verb, for example pods is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa" cannot list resource "pods" in the namespace "auth". Create the Role (the exact verb and resource) and the RoleBinding to that ServiceAccount; the Pod does not need to restart.

5Admission control

After authorization, admission controllers can change (mutating) or refuse (validating) the object. Several are on by default, and you have already met three:

Admission step What it does Where you met it
ServiceAccount puts the default ServiceAccount and the token volume into Pods this module
LimitRanger fills in default requests and limits, rejects values outside min and max Module 10
ResourceQuota rejects objects that would exceed the namespace quota Module 10
NamespaceLifecycle rejects objects in a namespace that is being deleted
PodSecurity enforces the Pod Security Standards by namespace label below
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy your own validation rules in CEL, without running a webhook below
webhooks MutatingWebhookConfiguration, ValidatingWebhookConfiguration call a service you run operators and policy engines

Pod Security Admission

The three Pod Security Standards are privileged (no restrictions), baseline (blocks the known privilege escalations: privileged containers, host namespaces, host paths, extra capabilities) and restricted (current hardening best practice: non-root user, no privilege escalation, drop all capabilities, a seccomp profile). A namespace label picks the mode and the level:

Label Mode Effect
pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline enforce violating Pods are rejected
pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=baseline warn the user gets a warning, the Pod is created
pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=baseline audit an audit-log annotation, the Pod is created 
k label namespace psa pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline
k label namespace psa pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite

Enforcement applies to new Pods: a Deployment whose template violates the standard is accepted, but its ReplicaSet cannot create Pods (forbidden: violates PodSecurity): read k describe rs. Module 12 shows the securityContext settings that satisfy restricted.

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy

A ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (stable API admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1) holds CEL expressions, for example "every Deployment must have at least 2 replicas", and a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding says where it applies. A rejected request returns the policy's message. For the CKAD you only need to recognize it and read its error.

Exam tip

. "Forbidden" means authorization (RBAC): fix it with a Role and a RoleBinding. "violates PodSecurity" or "exceeded quota" or "maximum cpu usage" means admission: fix the object or the namespace setting, not RBAC.

Exam tip

. Test every RBAC change with k auth can-i ... --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name> for a yes and for a no that must stay no.

6Lab tasks

<!-- LABS: m11 -->

Lab 11.1: serviceaccount pod

Domain: Environment | Points: 5 | Time: about 5 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m11-01-serviceaccount-pod)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace auth, create a ServiceAccount named app-sa. Create a Pod named client (image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600) that runs with that ServiceAccount. Wait until it is Running.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n auth create serviceaccount app-sa
kubectl -n auth run client --image=busybox:1.36 --dry-run=client -o yaml -- sleep 3600 > /tmp/client.yaml
sed -i 's/^spec:/spec:\n  serviceAccountName: app-sa/' /tmp/client.yaml
kubectl apply -f /tmp/client.yaml
kubectl -n auth wait --for=condition=Ready pod/client --timeout=120s
kubectl -n auth get pod client -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'; echo

Lab 11.2: no token automount

Domain: Environment | Points: 6 | Time: about 6 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m11-02-no-token-automount)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace auth, the ServiceAccount app-sa exists. Create a Pod named quiet (image busybox:1.36, command sleep 3600) that runs with app-sa but does not get an API token mounted into its containers (the directory /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount must not exist in the container). Do this in the Pod, not by changing the ServiceAccount.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n auth apply -f - <<'Y'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: quiet}
spec:
  serviceAccountName: app-sa
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
Y
kubectl -n auth wait --for=condition=Ready pod/quiet --timeout=120s
kubectl -n auth exec quiet -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount || echo "no token directory"

Lab 11.3: role rolebinding

Domain: Environment | Points: 8 | Time: about 8 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m11-03-role-rolebinding)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace auth, the ServiceAccount app-sa exists. Create a Role named pod-reader that allows only get, list and watch on Pods, and a RoleBinding named read-pods that gives this Role to app-sa. Afterwards the ServiceAccount must be able to list Pods in auth but not delete them, and must not be able to list Pods in the namespace default.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n auth create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods
kubectl -n auth create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=auth:app-sa
kubectl -n auth auth can-i delete pods --as=system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa
kubectl -n auth auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa

Lab 11.4: clusterrole rolebinding

Domain: Environment | Points: 7 | Time: about 7 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m11-04-clusterrole-rolebinding)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

The ClusterRole deploy-viewer (get and list on Deployments) already exists. In the namespace auth, give it to the ServiceAccount app-sa with a binding named view-deploys, so that app-sa can list Deployments in auth only. It must not be able to list Deployments in the namespace other.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n auth create rolebinding view-deploys --clusterrole=deploy-viewer --serviceaccount=auth:app-sa
kubectl -n other auth can-i list deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa
kubectl -n auth auth can-i list deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:auth:app-sa

Lab 11.5: create token

Domain: Environment | Points: 5 | Time: about 5 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m11-05-create-token)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace auth, the ServiceAccount app-sa exists. Create a token for it that is valid for exactly 2 hours, and write the token (just the token string) to ~/answers/token.txt on the host where you run kubectl.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n auth create token app-sa --duration=2h > ~/answers/token.txt
cut -d. -f2 ~/answers/token.txt | head -c 60; echo

Lab 11.6: fix forbidden api call

Domain: Environment | Points: 8 | Time: about 9 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m11-06-fix-forbidden-api-call)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

In the namespace auth, the Pod caller (ServiceAccount app-sa) asks the API server every 3 seconds for the list of Pods in its own namespace and prints the HTTP status code. It prints 403. Without changing the Pod, give its ServiceAccount exactly the access it needs, namely list on Pods in the namespace auth (use a Role named pod-lister and a RoleBinding named pod-lister-binding), so that the log shows 200.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl -n auth logs caller | tail -2
kubectl -n auth create role pod-lister --verb=list --resource=pods
kubectl -n auth create rolebinding pod-lister-binding --role=pod-lister --serviceaccount=auth:app-sa
sleep 6
kubectl -n auth logs caller | tail -2

Lab 11.7: pod security admission

Domain: Environment | Points: 7 | Time: about 7 minutes | Status: executed and validated on Kubernetes v1.37.0 (id m11-07-pod-security-admission)

Context: kubectl config use-context kind-ckad

The namespace psa exists. Make the cluster reject Pods that violate the baseline Pod Security Standard in that namespace (enforce it with a namespace label, not just a warning). Then create a Pod named ok (image nginx:alpine), which must be accepted and Running. A privileged Pod must now be rejected in psa.

Reference solution (try the task first; on the exam ssh <node> replaces the lab's docker exec):

kubectl label namespace psa pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline
kubectl -n psa run ok --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl -n psa wait --for=condition=Ready pod/ok --timeout=120s
kubectl -n psa apply -f - <<'Y' || echo "rejected as expected"
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: priv}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext: {privileged: true}
Y

<!-- /LABS -->

7Recall questions

R1What are the three gates of an API request, in order?

Show the answer

Authentication, authorization, admission control.

R2Which HTTP status means "not allowed" and which means "not authenticated"?

Show the answer

403 Forbidden is authorization; 401 Unauthorized is authentication.

R3What identity does a Pod's ServiceAccount have?

Show the answer

system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>.

R4How do you stop a Pod from receiving an API token?

Show the answer

automountServiceAccountToken: false in the Pod spec (or on the ServiceAccount).

R5What does a RoleBinding that references a ClusterRole do?

Show the answer

It grants the ClusterRole's rules only inside the binding's namespace.

R6Which command shows whether a ServiceAccount may delete Pods in a namespace?

Show the answer

kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>.

R7What do the Pod Security labels enforce, warn and audit do?

Show the answer

Enforce rejects violating Pods; warn shows a warning; audit records an audit annotation.

R8Can you create a deny rule in RBAC?

Show the answer

No; RBAC only adds permissions.

Quick Reference Card

Topic Remember
Gates authentication (401), authorization (403), admission (policy error)
ServiceAccount serviceAccountName, token in /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount, automountServiceAccountToken
Token kubectl create token <sa> --duration=2h
RBAC Role/ClusterRole + RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding; additive
Create create role --verb --resource, create rolebinding --role (or --clusterrole) --serviceaccount=ns:name
Test kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> -n <ns> --as=...
Admission ServiceAccount, LimitRanger, ResourceQuota, PodSecurity, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, webhooks
Pod Security namespace labels enforce/warn/audit with privileged/baseline/restricted
